Apply within 12 months to rejoin the EU under a bespoke Sovereignty Protocol: retain the pound indefinitely via a formal opt-out from euro adoption; remain outside Schengen with a treaty-based emergency brake (modeled on EEA Article 112) allowing time-limited quotas on intra-EU labour inflows when objective thresholds for public-service capacity are exceeded; accept ECJ jurisdiction limited to single-market matters; commit to full budget contributions and regulatory alignment. A cross-party negotiating mandate will codify these red lines and require quarterly transparency reports. Trade-off: the EU may resist permanent free-movement derogations and euro opt-outs, prolonging talks and risking failure to conclude an accession treaty.

Pass an EU Rejoin Referendum Act scheduling, within 18 months, a binding referendum on whether the UK should rejoin the EU on standard accession terms (acceptance of the acquis, free movement of people, ECJ authority, budget contributions, and a commitment in principle to adopt the euro when convergence criteria are met, with no bespoke UK-only opt-outs beyond those available to current members). An independent information process (citizens’ panel-vetted booklet, strict spending caps, and broadcast standards enforcement) will precede the vote; a simple nationwide majority determines the outcome. Trade-off: a contentious campaign and elevated policy uncertainty until the vote.

Legislate a five-year Non-Rejoin Stabilization Plan that rules out applying to rejoin before 2031 while implementing a UK–EU Sectoral Accords Package: a Medicines and Medical Devices mutual recognition agreement with joint procurement to safeguard supply; an SPS/veterinary agreement to cut agrifood checks by at least 80%; expedited mutual recognition of health and care qualifications; a Charitable Goods Corridor with customs/VAT waivers; and a reciprocal Shortage Occupation Mobility Scheme offering capped two-year work visas in priority sectors. Establish a £2 billion annual Stabilization Fund for workforce training and port/IT upgrades. Trade-off: ongoing frictions and partial regulatory alignment without a formal vote or influence over EU rulemaking.

The UK will apply to rejoin the European Union within 12 months under Article 49, with a domestic mandate to accept the acquis, freedom of movement, ECJ jurisdiction, and customs union membership; seek a Schengen opt-out; commit to retain sterling (no euro adoption or ERM II entry during the first 10 years); pass an EU Restoration Bill to pre-align key regulations, create an Office for EU Transition to address labor shortages and business support, and hold a binding confirmatory referendum on the final accession treaty.

The UK will pursue the Norway model: apply for EFTA membership and negotiate EEA participation within 18 months, restoring single-market access for goods, services, capital, and people while remaining outside EU institutions and the customs union; adopt relevant single-market rules, pay EEA contributions, implement an emergency safeguard for temporary labor-market pressures, conclude a UK-EU SPS/veterinary agreement to reduce GB-NI and GB-EU border checks, and include a statutory five-year review offering options to remain EEA, add a customs union, or proceed to EU accession talks.

The government will rule out applying to rejoin the EU in the next Parliament and instead enact an EU Relations Stabilisation Plan: agree a reciprocal UK-EU Youth and Skills Mobility Scheme (ages 18-30, two-year visas, capped numbers), negotiate a legally binding SPS/veterinary accord and trusted-trader expansion to ease NI and Dover trade frictions, create a hospitality and tourism shortage occupation route, establish an independent statutory inquiry into the conduct and accuracy of the 2016 referendum, and convene a citizens' assembly to define criteria and a decision point in 2030 for any future rejoin talks or referendum.

The government will enact a Rejoin Mandate Act establishing: (a) an 18-month pre-application negotiation with the EU to publish a draft accession framework (budget contribution phasing, citizens' rights, Ireland arrangements, transition periods for acquis adoption); (b) an independent cost-benefit audit laid before Parliament; and (c) a legally binding double-majority referendum in 2029 (UK-wide majority and a simple majority in each of England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland). Only if the referendum passes will the UK submit an application to rejoin; the Act acknowledges likely loss of former opt-outs and higher net contributions as tradeoffs for market access and institutional voice.

Parliament will pass a Sovereign Renewal and Rural Stewardship Act establishing a 15-year moratorium (until 2041) on any application to rejoin the EU, while mitigating Brexit frictions via: a UK-EU sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) equivalence treaty to cut border checks; GBP 2.0 billion over 10 years for hedgerow restoration and traditional orchard replanting grants; a UK label of origin and standards regime for food; and a Border Efficiency Fund to digitize customs for SMEs. Tradeoffs include reduced regulatory alignment limiting deeper market access and ongoing administrative costs.

The UK will not apply to rejoin but will seek a Bridge Compact with the EU by 2027: a permanent customs union on goods (excluding agriculture unless SPS alignment is agreed), dynamic alignment in limited sectors (chemicals, aviation safety, data), mutual recognition of professional qualifications, re-entry to Erasmus-style student exchanges, and a youth mobility/work scheme capped at 25,000 visas per side annually; disputes would use independent arbitration with references to the ECJ only on EU law points; the UK would make a proportional annual financial contribution. Tradeoffs include constrained rule-making autonomy and budget payments in exchange for lower trade barriers and mobility.

The government will legislate for a 2-stage, legally binding process in the next Parliament: (1) an 18-month Independent EU Membership Commission to publish audited impact assessments (trade, regions, public finances, migration, rights, security, Northern Ireland) and two detailed policy packages—A: apply to rejoin the EU under a published negotiating mandate; B: remain outside with a defined cooperation package—supported by citizens’ assemblies in all four nations; (2) a national referendum 3 months after the Commission’s final report with a single, clear question choosing between Package A or B, with campaign finance caps, real-time donation disclosure, equal airtime, an official voter guide, and online ad transparency. Franchise: UK citizens and settled residents aged 16+, with accessible voting provisions; result requires a simple UK-wide majority and separate advisory thresholds published for each nation to inform inter-governmental implementation. Trade-off: longer timeline and temporary uncertainty in exchange for an informed, rules-based mandate.

The UK will adopt an Article 49 Rejoin Mandate and Alignment Roadmap: within 6 months, Parliament passes a European Alignment Act restoring EU-compatible rules in goods SPS, chemicals (REACH), data, state aid, aviation, and financial regulation; the government applies for association to Horizon Europe and Erasmus+, and seeks a comprehensive SPS/veterinary agreement and a youth mobility scheme with the EU as pre-accession confidence-building steps; after 24 months of alignment, the UK submits a formal application to rejoin the EU, accepting freedom of movement, budget contributions, ECJ jurisdiction in areas of EU law, and a commitment to meet euro convergence criteria without a fixed adoption date, while preserving the Common Travel Area. A £5bn Re-Entry Transition Fund supports sectors facing adjustment (e.g., fisheries, customs brokerage). Trade-off: reduced regulatory autonomy and fiscal contributions in exchange for Single Market access and investment certainty.

The government will rule out applying to rejoin the EU for 10 years via a Stability and EU Cooperation Act, and instead implement a targeted mitigation package: negotiate a legally binding UK–EU SPS/veterinary accord to cut GB–EU food checks by 80%, a mutual recognition of conformity assessment for low-risk manufactured goods, a structured equivalence regime for financial services with joint dispute panels, full association to Horizon Europe and a reciprocal youth mobility scheme, and a permanent green-lane expansion for NI–GB trade with trusted trader status. Domestically, create a single customs window, a £2bn Port Modernisation Fund, and a shortage-occupation skills visa to ease trade frictions. An annual OBR-audited impact report to Parliament will track outcomes and allow course corrections short of re-application. Trade-off: continued frictions versus policy certainty and focused investment.

Pursue EEA membership via EFTA within 24 months to restore broad single market access without joining the customs union, accepting free movement, dynamic alignment with relevant EU law, and EFTA Court oversight; introduce an EEA Accession Bill setting negotiation objectives, create an EEA Implementation Authority to audit and update UK statutes, conclude an EU‑UK veterinary and plant health agreement to remove most agri‑food checks, and establish a five‑year 5 billion pounds Transition Support Fund for SMEs, fisheries, and regulators; tradeoffs include budget contributions, reduced regulatory autonomy, and compliance costs.

Rule out applying to rejoin the EU or the single market for at least 10 years through a No Rejoin Stability Act, and instead implement a UK‑EU competitiveness package comprising a mutual recognition agreement for conformity assessment in key manufacturing and chemicals, expanded rules of origin cumulation, a comprehensive veterinary and plant health agreement, permanent Horizon Europe association and a reciprocal youth mobility scheme, an expanded trusted trader green lane under the Windsor Framework, and a 2 billion pounds Customs Digitalisation Programme to cut border friction; this provides certainty and lowers trade costs while accepting ongoing barriers and limits to market access.

Adopt a conditional EU reaccession roadmap culminating in a national referendum in 2030: establish a 2026 Royal Commission to assess economic, legal, and constitutional implications; pass a 2027 Negotiating Mandate Act authorising exploratory talks on accession terms including time‑limited derogations and transition periods for euro adoption and Schengen implementation, preservation of the Common Travel Area with Ireland, and measures to settle Northern Ireland trade frictions; in 2028–2029 align priority regulations in chemicals, data, and product standards, create a Reaccession Transition Fund, and publish an EU budget contribution forecast; if an accession treaty is agreed, put it to a legally binding referendum with a clear accept or reject question; risks include business adjustment costs and uncertainty during the transition.

The UK will open formal exploratory talks with the European Commission in 2026 to define a draft accession package (budget contribution band, restoration of full freedom of movement, ECJ jurisdiction, CAP/CFP participation, and regulatory realignment in goods, SPS, data, and financial services), publish the negotiated terms by mid-2028, and hold a legally binding referendum in October 2028 on rejoining the EU on those terms; to signal credibility, the UK will pre-align SPS rules and reintroduce mutual recognition of CE marking by 2027, and establish a transitional budget reserve equivalent to 0.15% of GDP to cover contributions; trade-offs include reduced unilateral regulatory control and direct fiscal contributions in exchange for single market access and mobility.

The government will legislate a 10-year moratorium (2025-2035) on applying to rejoin the EU, while executing a Europe Cooperation Package to mitigate frictions: negotiate a veterinary/SPS agreement to reduce border checks on agri-food, a UK-EU Youth Mobility and Professional Recognition scheme with capped visas (e.g., 30,000 per year) and mutual qualification recognition in health and engineering, deepen customs data-sharing and trusted trader schemes to cut small-firm paperwork, rejoin Erasmus+ and expand Horizon Europe participation, and invest GBP 3bn in port infrastructure and SME customs digitisation; this preserves border and immigration control but accepts continued rule divergence costs and foregoes voting rights in EU rulemaking.

Adopt an EEA Bridge Strategy whereby the UK seeks EFTA membership and re-enters the European Economic Area by 2027 to regain single market access while remaining outside the EU's political institutions, with a statutory five-year review in 2032 offering a choice between remaining in the EEA or holding a referendum on full EU membership; this entails accepting free movement, most single-market rules, budget contributions, and surveillance by the EFTA Court, trading voting power for economic integration and supply-chain stability.

The UK will apply in 2027 to rejoin the EU with a negotiating mandate that seeks: (1) retention of the pound sterling indefinitely; (2) formal non-participation in Schengen; (3) a time-limited Free Movement Safeguard enabling emergency caps on new EU workers in sectors under stress for up to 7 years; (4) full re-entry to the single market, customs union, Horizon, and Erasmus; (5) acceptance of ECJ oversight in single-market matters; (6) standard budget contributions; and (7) deepened defence cooperation while retaining sovereign command of UK forces. Justification: restores frictionless trade and research ties while addressing border and currency concerns. Tradeoffs: low likelihood of securing euro and migration opt-outs could prolong talks; higher budget costs and reduced unilateral regulatory autonomy.

The UK will legislate to rule out applying to rejoin the EU for the next two parliaments and instead deliver a TCA+ 2.0 package by 2027: dynamic alignment with EU SPS rules to remove most agri-food checks; mutual recognition of professional qualifications in priority sectors; a reciprocal youth mobility scheme (age 18–30, 2-year visas, capped at 30,000 each way); rejoining Erasmus+ and associate membership of Horizon Europe; a customs green-lane program for trusted traders at Dover–Calais; and a UK–EU Security Council for data sharing and policing. Justification: secures practical benefits without membership uncertainty. Tradeoffs: continued exclusion from full single-market rights, limited say over rule-making, and ongoing border formalities for non-aligned sectors.

The UK will pass a Rejoin Roadmap Act establishing a two-step democratic process: a 12-month Citizens’ Assembly and cross-party convention to draft an accession White Paper (accepting the acquis and ECJ jurisdiction in relevant areas, remaining outside Schengen like Ireland, retaining GBP until euro convergence criteria are met, and phasing in free movement and regulatory alignment over 5 years), followed by a binding referendum in 2028 requiring a 55% UK-wide majority and simple majorities in England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland. If approved, the government will submit an application in 2029; if rejected, it will codify long-term non-membership and upgrade the TCA. Justification: clear mandate before negotiations. Tradeoffs: longer timeline, administrative cost, and a higher threshold that may make change harder.

Legislate a two‑stage Rejoin Decision Process: 1) establish an Independent EU Impact Commission (with OBR-style statutory independence) to publish audited reports on economic, social, security, and diplomatic impacts of rejoining versus not rejoining, including effects on the EU and key trading partners; run UK-wide citizens’ assemblies and require a government Green Paper and a parliamentary White Paper responding to evidence within 12 months; 2) hold a first referendum to authorize an accession application, with a simple majority and a 60% turnout threshold; if authorized, adopt a cross‑party negotiating mandate (agreed with devolved governments) prioritizing Northern Ireland arrangements, the Common Travel Area with Ireland, budget contributions, free movement administration, and agency participation; once provisional terms are reached, hold a second confirmatory referendum on the negotiated package; include a four‑year sunset if talks stall. Tradeoff: longer timeline and policy uncertainty during negotiations.

Pursue a UK‑EU Goods Customs Union and SPS Alignment Treaty without EU membership: negotiate a legally binding customs union covering industrial goods and processed foods (removing tariffs and rules‑of‑origin), plus dynamic alignment to the EU sanitary and phytosanitary rulebook overseen by a joint committee and a limited CJEU reference mechanism for SPS disputes; expand the Windsor Framework green lanes to eliminate routine checks on GB‑NI goods destined for final consumption in NI; include reciprocal youth mobility visas (ages 18–30, two‑year stays, capped quotas), mutual recognition of professional qualifications in priority sectors (e.g., engineering, nursing), and data/market surveillance cooperation; make proportionate contributions to relevant EU agencies (EFSA, EMSA) and adopt a safeguard clause for serious divergence. Tradeoff: constrained regulatory autonomy on goods and ongoing financial contributions without a vote in EU rulemaking.

Enact a statutory 10‑year moratorium on applying to rejoin the EU and fund a domestic adjustment package: prohibit any accession application before 2036 unless overturned by a two‑thirds Commons vote; create a £5bn Border Modernisation Fund (Single Trade Window, end‑to‑end trusted trader expansion, interoperable SPS inspection tech) to cut compliance costs; negotiate deeper mutual recognition of Authorised Economic Operator status with the EU; launch a targeted regulatory divergence programme in three sectors (e.g., biotech, financial services, AI) with an independent adequacy/market‑access risk test before changes; expand the Turing Scheme and secure Erasmus+ youth exchanges via bilateral protocols; mandate triennial independent reviews on growth, prices, and trade frictions to adjust policy. Tradeoff: reduces strategic leverage with the EU and may increase frictions if divergence triggers EU safeguards.

Apply to rejoin the EU in 2026 with a staged accession plan: pass an EU Alignment Act to restore single-market and customs union rules in goods, SPS, chemicals, and data protection by 2027; negotiate an interim UK–EU customs union and a comprehensive SPS veterinary agreement to cut checks while accession proceeds; commit to Schengen entry within two years of accession and to euro convergence without a target date; accept ECJ jurisdiction and phase in full EU budget contributions over five years; hold a binding national referendum to ratify the accession treaty before entry into force. Tradeoffs: higher budget contributions and the return of free movement in exchange for reduced trade friction and restored influence in EU rule-making.

Pursue EEA membership via EFTA within 24 months and Schengen association thereafter: apply to join EFTA in year one; pass an EEA Accession Bill to adopt the EEA acquis for goods, services, capital, and free movement of people, with participation in the EEA Joint Committee and EFTA Court oversight; agree to EEA-style financial contributions and data-sharing obligations; upgrade border infrastructure and IT to integrate with Schengen information systems and ETIAS, with an application for Schengen association once EEA obligations are operational. Tradeoffs: rapid market access with minimal customs friction, but limited formal vote on EU rules and acceptance of free movement.

Launch a 2026–2030 UK–EU Deep Cooperation and Readiness Programme with a 2030 binding referendum on whether to apply to rejoin: negotiate a TCA-plus package including a veterinary and SPS agreement, mutual recognition of conformity assessment for key sectors, a reciprocal youth mobility scheme for ages 18–30, rejoining Erasmus Plus, enhanced law-enforcement data sharing, and streamlined professional qualification recognition; establish an independent Reaccession Readiness Commission to report annually on regulatory alignment, customs performance, migration flows, and fiscal impacts; commit in law to hold a binding referendum in 2030 on applying to rejoin, with the government obligated to submit an application within three months if the vote is affirmative. Tradeoffs: defers a rejoin decision while reducing current frictions, but prolongs uncertainty for businesses and investors.

Apply to rejoin the EU with a bespoke accession protocol: (1) remain outside Schengen to preserve UK border controls while maintaining the Common Travel Area with Ireland; (2) retain the pound indefinitely by not entering ERM II, acknowledging the legal obligation to work toward euro adoption without a timetable; (3) negotiate an emergency safeguard, pre-approved by the Commission and Council, permitting temporary, targeted limits on free movement of workers into defined localities for up to three years during exceptional labour market or public service pressures; (4) re-enter the customs union and single market upon provisional application of the accession treaty, with a five-year transition to adopt the acquis and limited sectoral derogations (e.g., fisheries management and procurement thresholds); (5) commit to a transparent budget contribution schedule and an Accession Unit to manage legal alignment. Tradeoff: unprecedented safeguards may be resisted by EU institutions, risking slower or partial accession.

Legislate a 10-year Stability and Market Access Plan ruling out an EU rejoin application for two parliamentary terms while deepening ties under the Trade and Cooperation Agreement: negotiate an SPS/veterinary equivalence deal to cut food import costs, a capped youth mobility and short-term work scheme, a Services Access Accord (data adequacy extensions, professional qualifications, regulatory dialogue), and mutual recognition for conformity assessment in selected manufacturing; implement a single customs portal with expanded trusted trader status and a £2bn Border Efficiency Fund; enact five-year, reviewable dynamic alignment in chemicals, automotive and agri-food to reduce non-tariff barriers; create a UK–EU Joint Economic Council to manage disputes and upgrades. Tradeoff: targeted alignment constrains regulatory autonomy but reduces costs and avoids reopening a polarising accession process.

Mandate a 2028 two-path referendum with pre-published terms: the government conducts 12–18 months of prenegotiations to produce (A) an Accession Package (non-participation in Schengen with CTA preserved, retention of the pound via no ERM II entry, phased re-entry to CAP/CFP with transitional quotas, rejoining Horizon and Erasmus-style programmes, and an OBR-certified budget contribution profile) and (B) an Enhanced Partnership Package (SPS deal, mobility scheme, services accord, conformity assessment mutual recognition, and customs modernisation), each with independent impact assessments; the referendum is binding with a 60% turnout requirement and a majority in at least three UK nations; enabling legislation for either outcome is pre-drafted with clear implementation timetables. Tradeoff: longer timeline and administrative cost, but delivers clarity and immediate implementability whichever path is chosen.

The UK will submit an application to rejoin the European Union in 2026, accepting the four freedoms and ECJ jurisdiction, with a 24-month Acquis Alignment Plan to re-enter the customs union and single market by 2028; a £10bn Reintegration and Resilience Fund will support local housing, GP capacity, and skills in areas experiencing rapid growth from renewed freedom of movement; the UK will rejoin Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe immediately upon association offers, and implement an EU-law screening unit in the Cabinet Office to manage transposition; trade-offs include annual budget contributions, reduced unilateral regulatory autonomy, and transitional costs for firms adjusting back to EU rules.

The government will seek EFTA membership and EEA re-entry within 18 months as an interim step, restoring single market access and freedom of movement under EEA rules and EFTA Court oversight, paired with a Domestic Capacity Guarantee that channels hypothecated visa and employer levies into local services; a legally binding referendum on full EU membership will be held in 2029 contingent on publication of accession terms, with a 55% supermajority and 60% turnout threshold to reverse the 2016 decision; trade-offs include paying into EU programs without a vote at the EU table during the EEA phase and prolonged uncertainty if accession talks stall.

The UK will rule out applying to rejoin the EU for the next Parliament and instead implement a 5-year UK–EU Stabilisation Package: a comprehensive SPS/veterinary agreement to cut border checks on agri-food; mutual recognition of conformity assessment in limited sectors; a trusted trader/green lane scheme with digitised customs for SMEs; a reciprocal Youth Mobility and Frontier Worker scheme (ages 18–30, capped quotas, 2-year stays); fast-track mutual recognition of professional qualifications in health and engineering; and targeted export and recruitment support for the NHS and care sector; trade-offs include continued tariffs outside the customs union, ongoing paperwork for many sectors, and no automatic rights for UK citizens to live and work across the EU.

Enact an 8-year Stability and Review Act that rules out applying to rejoin the EU before 2034, while maximizing practical cooperation and reducing trade frictions. The Act would: (a) create an independent Office for Post‑Brexit Evaluation to publish annual, sector-by-sector impact reports and a five-year comprehensive review; (b) mandate targeted UK–EU accords (veterinary/SPS alignment to cut agri-food checks, mutual recognition for professional qualifications where feasible, a mobility scheme for young people and researchers, data and security cooperation upgrades, dual CE/UKCA conformity marking for defined sectors); (c) fund a small‑exporter support scheme to help firms navigate rules of origin; (d) require a two‑thirds Commons vote to lift the moratorium early. Tradeoffs: forecloses near-term rejoin but reduces uncertainty; sectoral alignment may constrain domestic regulatory divergence and entail limited programme contributions.

Pursue an EEA/EFTA ‘Norway model’ within three years as a structured pathway to restore single‑market access without full EU membership. The government would seek EFTA accession (subject to EFTA states’ consent) and negotiate: (a) EEA entry with acceptance of the four freedoms, budget contributions, and regulatory alignment; (b) a parallel veterinary/SPS agreement and a customs facilitation package to ease border checks; (c) a financial services equivalence and supervisory cooperation framework; (d) re‑entry to Horizon Europe and a UK–EU youth mobility scheme; (e) a statutory domestic safeguard allowing temporary, evidence‑based labor market measures consistent with EEA rules; (f) retention of the pound, and a legal requirement that any future euro adoption must be approved by a separate UK referendum. Include a year‑6 review with a public report and a referendum option on full EU accession. Tradeoffs: material rule‑taking and fiscal contributions with limited formal vote, but reduced trade frictions and improved services access.

Pass a Conditional Re‑accession and Referendum Act that authorizes the government to negotiate, within 18 months, an agreed ‘heads of terms’ accession framework with the EU and puts the final decision to a national vote. Preconditions for the referendum: publication of (a) an in‑principle EU–UK framework covering budget contributions, a timetable for acquis alignment (24–36 months), justice and home affairs opt‑ins, Schengen cooperation without borderless entry, fisheries quota arrangements, Northern Ireland arrangements, and a financial services market access plan; (b) a legal opinion on euro adoption stating the UK would commit to convergence criteria but cannot adopt the euro without a separate UK referendum; (c) an independently audited macroeconomic and distributional impact assessment; (d) a six‑month UK‑wide citizens’ assembly process with televised hearings. The referendum would include a national turnout threshold and a double‑lock requiring a UK‑wide majority and a majority in at least three of the four nations. Tradeoffs: longer timeline and higher entry bar; EU may resist bespoke terms.

Pass a Sovereign Trade and Supply Act establishing a moratorium on applying to rejoin the EU until 2035 while intensifying global trade and domestic resilience: conclude FTAs with the United States and India by 2028; expand CPTPP utilization and digital customs to cut non-tariff barriers; invest £3bn in port/airport infrastructure and customs technology to streamline UK–EU and rest-of-world freight; introduce a three-year Food Staples Tariff Waiver for selected non-EU imports (e.g., certain fruits, grains) to ease prices; and launch a £1bn export support scheme for services and agri-food to non-EU markets, maintaining the TCA without new regulatory alignment commitments that constrain third-country deals. Trade-offs include reduced leverage in EU talks, pressure on some domestic producers from cheaper imports, and closing the near-term reapplication window.

Negotiate a UK–EU Enhanced Cooperation Treaty to lower frictions without membership: agree sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) equivalence with optional dynamic alignment in food safety to cut checks and spoilage; mutually recognize professional qualifications in priority sectors; implement trusted-trader Green Lanes at UK–EU borders and the Irish Sea with joint customs data-sharing and risk-based inspections; fully participate in Horizon Europe and a reciprocal youth mobility scheme (18–30, two-year stays, capped quotas) on a cost-share basis; and target a 40% reduction in average UK–EU clearance times within two years. Trade-offs include partial regulatory alignment, programme contributions, and administrative costs.

Introduce an EU Options Review and Referendum Act with a conditional 2029 decision point: establish an independent commission to publish a fiscal, regulatory, and migration impact assessment comparing (a) an upgraded cooperation package and (b) full EU re-accession; authorize a non-binding exploratory mandate to the EU to scope accession parameters (budget contributions and free movement, seeking retention of previous opt-outs from the euro and Schengen) without triggering Article 49; require that no application be submitted unless approved in a national referendum held between April and October 2029, with a negotiated cooperation alternative on the ballot; and set impartial information rules and spending caps. Trade-offs include business uncertainty, political polarisation risk, and potential EU reluctance to pre-negotiate.

The UK will apply to rejoin the EU on a conditional mandate: retain the pound permanently; remain outside Schengen with full border checks; secure a treaty protocol limiting access to non-contributory in-work benefits for new EU arrivals for up to four years and allowing temporary regional safeguard measures during severe labour market shocks; accept CAP and CFP with a seven-year transition that prioritises CAP eco-schemes for hedgerow and traditional orchard restoration and a phased fisheries quota rebalancing; and pass a Great Reaccession Act to align EU law with scheduled parliamentary sunset reviews. If these terms are not agreed within 24 months, the mandate lapses without accession.

Parliament will enact a 15-year moratorium on any application to rejoin the EU and instead negotiate a UK–EU Practical Cooperation Package: a veterinary and plant health accord to reduce border checks, a capped and reciprocal youth mobility scheme, associate participation in data and chemicals regimes, streamlined conformity assessment for low-risk goods, and a reinforced security liaison treaty; domestically, a £1.5bn Hedgerows and Orchards Restoration Fund with statutory net-gain targets by 2040. This avoids reaccession while reducing trade friction and supporting rural recovery, at the cost of ongoing regulatory duplication and UK budget outlays.

The government will run a two-stage, legally binding process: within 12 months, a mandate referendum asking whether to authorise negotiations to rejoin the EU under a published white paper that commits to keeping the pound and remaining outside Schengen; if authorised, an 18-month negotiation followed by a confirmatory referendum on the final accession treaty requiring both a double majority across UK nations and a 60 percent turnout threshold. This seeks informed consent but extends uncertainty and constrains negotiating flexibility.

Enact a Rejoin Moratorium and Global Markets Act: a statutory bar on applying to rejoin the EU until 2033, paired with a GBP 15 billion, 5-year plan to cut trade frictions and food costs without EU membership. Measures include full digitization of customs and SPS checks at major ports, port automation grants and around-the-clock veterinary capacity at Dover and Holyhead, bilateral SPS equivalence deals with key non-EU suppliers, an agri-productivity fund for cold-chain and glasshouse upgrades, and expansion of trusted trader and AEO-based fast lanes with the EU under the Trade and Cooperation Agreement. Government will publish annual metrics (clearance times, grocery CPI contribution, SME export volumes) and sunset the package in 2033. Tradeoff: foregoes potential single-market benefits in the medium term and requires upfront public spending.

Pursue EEA membership via EFTA and accede to the Schengen Area on an expedited but sequenced timeline (target within 36 months). The government will apply to EFTA, negotiate EEA participation accepting free movement, single-market rule alignment in goods and services, proportional budget contributions, and EFTA Court oversight on internal market matters. In parallel, negotiate a UK-EU customs facilitation treaty to simplify rules of origin and mutually recognize AEO schemes, and conclude an SPS alignment agreement to reduce food checks. Border systems will be upgraded to integrate Schengen (SIS, EES, ETIAS) with investment in biometric infrastructure and data safeguards. Tradeoff: recurring contributions and reduced regulatory autonomy in exchange for near-single-market access and eased travel.

Legislate a two-stage EU re-accession process for 2028-2032. Stage 1 (Q4 2028): a national referendum to mandate the government to negotiate EU re-entry under conditions that include acceptance of the acquis, ECJ jurisdiction where applicable, budget contributions, and free movement; no commitment to adopt the euro within the next two parliamentary terms, acknowledging EU treaty requirements on eventual adoption. Stage 2 (upon conclusion of talks, no later than 2032): a binding ratification referendum on the negotiated treaty. From 2026, a cross-party commission will prepare domestic alignment in SPS, REACH, aviation safety, and data adequacy; create a Migration Capacity Fund for housing, skills, and primary care; and explore an interim UK-EU customs union to cut border costs for food and manufacturing during talks. Tradeoff: loss of independent tariff policy and higher fiscal contributions versus reduced trade frictions and regulatory clarity.

The UK government will submit an Article 49 application to rejoin the EU in Q4 2026, accompanied by an EU Re-Entry Bill that restores alignment with the acquis, accepts free movement, CJEU jurisdiction, and standard budget contributions, seeks a protocol preserving the Common Travel Area with Ireland, and defers euro adoption by not entering ERM II without a separate domestic vote; negotiations targeted at 18 months with a 12-month ratification window, accession aimed for 2029–2030, and a £3bn Transition Support Fund for sectors facing regulatory change; tradeoffs include fiscal contributions, migration inflows, and reduced unilateral rule-making.

The UK will pursue a two-step pathway by seeking EFTA membership and EEA accession within 24 months to restore single-market access while remaining outside the customs union, coupled with a veterinary/SPS agreement and mutual recognition for medicines and chemicals; Parliament will set a binding national referendum for June 2030 offering two choices—full EU reaccession on agreed terms or continued EEA/EFTA status—with the OBR publishing negotiated terms and quantified impacts six months in advance; tradeoffs include budget contributions, free movement, and rule-taking without a vote in EU institutions during the interim.

Parliament will enact a 10-year moratorium on applying to rejoin the EU and instead mandate a UK-EU Partnership 2.0 that upgrades the Trade and Cooperation Agreement via a youth mobility scheme (ages 18–30, capped visas), a comprehensive SPS deal to cut border checks by at least 80%, sectoral mutual recognition in pharmaceuticals and automotive standards, and streamlined professional qualifications, backed by a £5bn Competitiveness Fund and a statutory Sovereignty Impact Assessment for any future alignment; tradeoffs include persistent customs frictions, limited influence over EU rules, and lower long-term growth potential versus full membership.

The government will table an EU Reaccession Mandate Bill committing the UK to apply to rejoin the EU in a two-stage process: (1) within 12 months, align UK law with the EU acquis for goods, SPS, and customs, rejoin EU agencies (Europol, EMA, Erasmus+), and negotiate a customs union and data adequacy, accepting ECJ jurisdiction in those areas; (2) within 24-36 months, submit a formal accession application, with any treaty agreed put to a national referendum for ratification. The mandate will include an immigration transition: phased restoration of free movement over three years with a parliamentary safeguard mechanism in case of severe labor market disruption. Justification: reduces trade frictions (including at the Irish Sea), restores influence, and provides democratic consent; tradeoffs include budget contributions, reduced regulatory autonomy, and administrative transition costs.

The Sovereignty and Self-Reliance Act will impose a 10-year statutory moratorium on any application to rejoin the EU (overturnable only by a two-thirds Commons majority), and instead direct funds to domestic alternatives: a £3bn Great British Land & Food Programme to restore 300,000 km of hedgerows and replant traditional orchards, a UK Standards and Recognition regime unilaterally accepting CE-marked goods to lower import frictions while maintaining domestic rule-making, and a Border 2.0 plan to simplify trader processes. The government will prioritize bilateral deals with EFTA states and deepen CPTPP participation, plus a targeted skills and seasonal worker visa to address labor gaps without free movement. Tradeoffs: continued customs paperwork with the EU, limited services access, and making future reaccession more complex, in return for full policy control and cultural autonomy.

The government will convene a 100-member Citizens’ Assembly on Europe for 12 months and in parallel seek from the EU a non-binding outline of accession terms (budget share, EU agency participation, justice and home affairs opt-ins, euro and Schengen opt-outs, migration transition). Within 18 months it will legislate for a binding ranked-choice referendum offering three options: (A) apply to rejoin on the outlined terms, (B) join EEA/EFTA with regulatory alignment in the single market but outside the customs union, or (C) retain the current Trade and Cooperation Agreement and pursue a sovereignty programme. The government will publish audited impact assessments for each path and commit to implement the winning option within 24 months. Tradeoffs: cost and uncertainty during the process, but allows an informed and decisive national choice.

EU Reaccess Referendum and Information Integrity Act: Parliament will legislate for a binding national referendum in Q2 2027 on whether the UK should apply to rejoin the EU, preceded by a 12-month independent evidence program (ONS, OBR, NAO) and an arm's-length Information Integrity Commission with powers to sanction materially misleading campaign claims; the franchise will include 16-17 year olds and UK citizens abroad; the result will require a 55% national majority and separate simple majorities in England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland; if 'Apply' wins, cross-party negotiating objectives must be tabled within 90 days; trade-off: higher thresholds reduce volatility but make change harder.

UK-EU Agri-Food and NI Stabilisation Package (no rejoin application): The UK will seek a 5-year, renewable sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) alignment agreement with the EU, trusted-trader digital customs corridors, and joint market surveillance to eliminate most checks in the Irish Sea and reduce supply-chain frictions; domestically, create a GBP 3bn Farming Transition Fund and a statutory regulatory certainty schedule locking agri-food standards for five years; trade-off: alignment limits UK rule-making flexibility in agri-food but materially eases NI and farming uncertainty.

Conditional EU Reaccess Application with Business Transition Guarantees: The government will submit an application to rejoin the EU no later than 2028, seeking to retain the UK's euro opt-out and the Common Travel Area with Ireland and to negotiate a 5-year migration implementation period within EU law; create a GBP 10bn Reaccess Transition Fund for SMEs, phased regulatory changeover windows by sector (12-36 months), and statutory tax credits for sunk Brexit compliance costs; trade-offs: budget contributions, ECJ jurisdiction, and restoration of free movement in exchange for frictionless trade and simpler supply chains.

Enact an EU Rejoin Moratorium Act (2026–2036) ruling out any application to rejoin the EU for 10 years, coupled with a Sovereignty and Supply Plan: conclude a UK–EU veterinary/SPS equivalence agreement to cut border checks on food and medicine; create a fast‑track NHS and social care visa to fill critical vacancies without restoring freedom of movement; launch a £1.5bn Hedgerow and Traditional Orchard Restoration Scheme to support farmers in replanting hedgerows and apple orchards and enhancing biodiversity; and replace retained EU agri‑environment rules with UK standards tailored to local conditions. Tradeoff: limited access gains to the single market and new budget costs, with continued customs frictions on most goods.

Legislate for a two‑stage democratic mandate to rejoin the EU: (1) a 2028 referendum asking whether to authorize the government to seek EU membership under a published negotiating mandate (single market and customs union participation, acceptance of freedom of movement, adherence to the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights, cooperation on security and research, maintenance of the Common Travel Area with Ireland, and a commitment not to enter ERM II during the first decade after accession); and (2) a confirmatory referendum on the final Article 49 accession treaty before ratification. An independent fiscal, trade, and migration impact assessment will be published before each vote, and a cross‑party committee will oversee talks. Tradeoff: higher budget contributions and regulatory alignment, with timelines contingent on EU agreement.

Apply to join EFTA and the EEA within 24 months as an interim step, substantially reducing regulatory frictions in goods and services trade (while accepting customs formalities) and restoring freedom of movement under EEA rules overseen by the EFTA Court; align UK product, food‑safety, and professional‑recognition rules with the EU acquis in single‑market areas; negotiate a parallel UK–EU veterinary/SPS agreement to minimize GB–NI and Dover–Calais checks; and legislate for a 2031 review and nationwide referendum on whether to proceed from EEA membership to full EU membership via an Article 49 application. Tradeoff: rule‑taking and budget contributions without a vote in EU institutions until full membership is pursued.

EU Membership Referendum and Information Integrity Act: Mandate a binding national referendum within 18 months with a clear two-option ballot—(A) apply to rejoin the EU under Article 49 or (B) maintain and deepen the current UK–EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement; extend the franchise to 16–17-year-olds and UK citizens abroad up to 30 years; create a statutory Independent Referendum Information Office to publish neutral impact assessments (OBR/NAO/BoE), archive and label all digital ads, ban foreign funding, and issue corrections for adjudicated false claims; set a 60% turnout floor and simple-majority outcome; if (A) wins, the government must apply within 3 months and introduce a preparatory alignment bill; if (B) wins, impose a 10-year moratorium on any application to rejoin. Tradeoffs: administrative cost and risk of renewed polarisation; a turnout floor could entrench the status quo if participation is low.

UK–EU Practical Cooperation and Supply Security Plan (No-Rejoin Lock): Enact a statute prohibiting any application to rejoin before 2035, while mandating a 2026 TCA upgrade to include (i) a comprehensive SPS/veterinary equivalence deal to ease border checks on food and medical ingredients, (ii) an MHRA–EMA mutual recognition agreement for batch testing and GMP inspections, (iii) UK association to Horizon’s successor and structured participation with HERA joint procurement for critical medical supplies, (iv) a targeted mobility package—two-year renewable health and social care visas, seasonal agriculture visas, a reciprocal youth mobility scheme—and automatic recognition of qualifications in shortage occupations, and (v) a 'Green Lane' customs regime for registered UK charities sending humanitarian aid to the EU. Tradeoffs: deeper alignment and mobility concessions reduce unilateral control, and benefits depend on EU willingness to conclude sectoral deals.

EU Reaccession Roadmap and Negotiation Mandate: Authorize application to rejoin within 6 months and set a negotiation mandate to (i) accept the EU acquis and CJEU jurisdiction with limited time‑bound derogations (up to 5 years), (ii) reintroduce free movement with domestic safeguards on abuse and swift removals, (iii) commit to EU budget contributions without a rebate and to euro adoption when convergence criteria are met (no fixed deadline), (iv) maintain the Common Travel Area with Ireland while phasing into Schengen-related systems (SIS participation and external border code alignment), (v) rejoin agencies and programmes (EMA, EASA, Europol, ECHA, Frontex, Erasmus+, ESF+), and (vi) establish a £5bn Reaccession Adjustment Fund to help firms and public services switch back to EU standards; require quarterly parliamentary reports and a final up‑or‑down ratification vote. Tradeoffs: higher fiscal contributions, immigration and regulatory shifts, and limited scope to negotiate opt‑outs compared with pre‑Brexit terms.

Rejoin Referendum Act 2028: Parliament will legislate for a legally binding referendum in June 2028 on whether the UK should apply to rejoin the EU, preceded by a 12-month Independent EU Impact Commission that publishes audited assessments of economic, social, security, devolution, and trading-partner impacts since 2016 and projected effects of rejoining vs. remaining outside. The Act mandates televised citizens’ assemblies in all UK nations with published summaries, equal campaign airtime and spending caps, strengthened misinformation penalties, donation transparency, and public data access. Franchise: UK citizens aged 16+, all UK-resident citizens of Ireland and Commonwealth countries as per current practice, and UK citizens abroad per the new lifetime voting rights. Result threshold: double-lock requiring (a) at least 55% UK-wide and (b) a simple majority in at least three of four nations. Enabling legislation is pre-drafted to submit an application within 90 days if approved. Tradeoff: higher threshold and longer timeline may delay or block change but aim to secure durable consent and robust evidence.

Accelerated Re-accession Application and Compliance Plan: Within six months, the Government will formally apply to rejoin the EU and publish a Compliance Plan committing to full acquis alignment, ECJ jurisdiction in EU law areas, and budget contributions under the standard formula. A dedicated Re-accession Unit will draft and pass enabling bills to re-align retained EU law (starting with customs, SPS, product standards, data, financial services equivalence), restore participation in Erasmus+ by 2026 and maintain association with Horizon Europe, and maintain the Windsor Framework until accession removes GB–EU trade frictions. The UK will seek an agreed phased restoration of reciprocal mobility and professional recognition during negotiations and set out a long-run pathway consistent with the EU’s requirements for euro adoption (without immediate adoption). Tradeoff: reduced unilateral regulatory autonomy and ongoing fiscal contributions in exchange for full single market access and institutional voice, with transitional adjustments for business and migration systems.

Decadal Stabilisation and Friction-Reduction Plan (No-Rejoin Moratorium): Parliament will enact a statutory moratorium on applying to rejoin the EU until 2036, while instructing the Government to negotiate a new UK–EU cooperation package: legally binding veterinary/SPS alignment to cut border checks, a streamlined customs and trusted-trader regime with single-window filings, a limited youth mobility and targeted skills visa scheme, expanded mutual recognition of professional qualifications in health, engineering, and finance, and durable financial services equivalence. Domestically, create a £3bn Export and Supply Chain Modernisation Fund for SMEs, digitise border infrastructure, and publish annual impact audits on trade, prices, and investment. Tradeoff: continued exclusion from EU decision-making and persistent non-tariff barriers in some sectors, in exchange for policy stability, lower administrative burden, and a focus on domestic competitiveness without reopening the membership question.

Sovereign Trade Deepening Plan (No-rejoin moratorium): Pass a 10-year statutory moratorium on applying to rejoin the EU, and redirect resources to a Global Market Access package: (a) conclude mutual recognition agreements in key sectors (chemicals, pharma, conformity assessment) with the US, Australia, India; (b) invest £5bn in customs modernization (single trade window, trusted trader schemes, digitized rules-of-origin tools) to cut border friction with EU and non-EU by 30%; (c) implement a two-year Food Import Cost Relief by suspending or lowering tariffs on selected staples to ease price pressures; (d) renew and expand UK–EU transport and haulage permits to keep links reliable. Trade-off: sustained regulatory divergence limits preferential EU access and keeps some checks in place.

EEA Accession Mandate (Norway model): Introduce legislation instructing the government to seek EFTA accession and EEA membership within 24 months, committing to dynamic alignment with single market rules, acceptance of free movement with a legally defined safeguard clause for local labor shocks, annual budget contributions capped as a share of GDP, mutual recognition of professional qualifications, and an SPS/customs cooperation chapter to remove most GB–EU goods checks; require a confirmatory referendum on the negotiated EEA terms before ratification. Trade-offs: limited formal vote on EU rulemaking, ongoing budget payments, constraints on state aid and regulatory autonomy.

Sequenced Rejoin Pathway with Benchmarks: Enact a four-year EU Relations Act that (1) creates an independent UK–EU Metrics Office to publish quarterly indicators on trade, investment, food prices, and border delays; (2) mandates immediate negotiations for a comprehensive veterinary/SPS agreement, a reciprocal youth mobility scheme, and full association to Horizon Europe; (3) establishes a cross-party council to prepare a potential reaccession mandate seeking assurances on currency and border controls; (4) schedules a binding national referendum in 2030 on applying to rejoin, contingent on published cooperation benchmarks. Trade-offs: prolonged uncertainty for firms and no guarantee the EU will grant preferred opt-outs.

Rejoin Moratorium and UK–EU Friction-Reduction Compact (2025–2035): Parliament will legislate a 10-year moratorium on applying to rejoin the EU, while implementing a £3bn package to cut trade frictions with the EU through a Swiss-style veterinary/SPS agreement to reduce agrifood checks, expansion of trusted trader schemes, a digital customs single window, targeted mutual recognition of professional qualifications in health, engineering, and finance, and a capped youth mobility scheme (two-year visas for ages 18–30, 20,000 places annually each way). The government will publish an annual impact report and a costed comparison of rejoin versus non-rejoin options. Tradeoff: partial regulatory alignment in covered sectors and continued budgetary and compliance costs without regaining EU voting rights.

Informed Mandate Referendum Act 2027: Establish an Independent Referendum Information Commission, run four citizens assemblies (one per UK nation), and require pre-referendum impact assessments from the OBR and Migration Advisory Committee. After a 12-month evidence period with enforced transparency and spending caps, hold a single-question vote in June 2027 on authorizing the government to apply to rejoin the EU. The result will be valid only with both a UK-wide majority and majorities in at least three of four nations; if passed, ministers must submit an Article 49 application within six months; if not, an eight-year cooling-off period applies. Tradeoff: longer timeline and administrative cost to ensure an informed and consent-based mandate.

Staged Re-accession via EEA Bridge (2027–2032): Seek EFTA accession in 2027 and enter the EEA by 2029 to restore single-market access, with dynamic regulatory alignment, EFTA Court oversight, and free movement subject to Article 112 safeguard mechanisms. In parallel, prepare an Article 49 EU application for 2030 with a negotiation mandate to accept the acquis, rejoin the customs union, CAP and CFP, contribute an estimated net £8–12bn annually, restore full participation in Horizon and Erasmus, seek a protocol preserving the Common Travel Area and an Ireland-style Schengen arrangement, and accept the obligation to adopt the euro in principle without a timetable. Conclude with a parliamentary vote and a confirmatory referendum before ratification. Tradeoff: reduced unilateral control over regulation and migration during the bridge period and fiscal costs ahead of regaining full EU decision-making rights.

Apply for EEA membership via EFTA by 2028 as a staging path to potential EU re-accession: immediately align UK sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) and product standards with the EU, conclude a veterinary and SPS agreement to reduce food checks and paperwork, rejoin Erasmus Plus, restore reciprocal freedom of movement under EEA rules to ease recruitment in shortage occupations (including NHS), and publish annual impact assessments on prices and trade. A national referendum in 2032 will decide on applying for full EU membership with a clear statement of obligations and costs. Trade-off: budget contributions, ECJ or EFTA Court oversight and reduced regulatory autonomy in exchange for lower trade frictions and improved labour mobility.

Legislate a 10-year moratorium on any EU membership application and implement a Sovereign Trade and Food Security Plan: expand the Single Trade Window and Trusted Trader schemes to halve customs paperwork by 2027, unilaterally recognize EU conformity assessments for low-risk goods, pursue targeted mutual recognition agreements in professional services, and launch a £1.2bn Traditional Landscapes and Orchards Fund under Environmental Land Management schemes to support hedgerow restoration and domestic fruit production. Create expanded sector-targeted visas (NHS, care, seasonal agriculture) alongside funded UK training bursaries. Trade-off: non-tariff barriers with the EU remain and some costs persist, but regulatory control and cultural autonomy are reinforced.

Hold a legally binding referendum in June 2028 on whether to apply to rejoin the EU under a published framework agreed in principle with the European Council: acceptance of the acquis, budget contributions, ECJ jurisdiction on relevant matters, phased two-year re-entry to the customs union and single market after application, and euro adoption only when convergence criteria are met. The ballot will offer a defined alternative UK-EU Partnership Package comprising a comprehensive SPS accord, a youth and skills mobility scheme with capped placements for health and social care, and enhanced customs cooperation and data sharing. Require a four-nation double majority and a 55 percent threshold to change the status quo. Trade-off: an extended timeline and uncertainty while options are prepared, in exchange for clarity and consent on concrete terms.

Rejoin Readiness and Application Plan (2027–2031): The UK will submit a formal application to rejoin the EU in 2027, coupled with a Rejoin Readiness Act aligning UK law with the EU acquis in priority areas (sanitary and phytosanitary rules, product standards, data protection, financial services equivalence). The plan reinstates full CE mark acceptance and phases out duplicative UKCA requirements by 2028, establishes a £3bn adjustment fund for SMEs and affected sectors, and reopens participation in Erasmus+ and EU research programs. The UK commits to free movement, ECJ jurisdiction where required, and standard budget contributions, with a domestic labour market transition package (skills, housing, and public service capacity funding). The Windsor Framework will be fully implemented to ensure frictionless movement across the Irish Sea. Trade-offs include loss of unilateral trade policy, budget contributions, and accepting EU rule-making without a national veto during the accession process.

Two-Stage Referendum with Statutory Facts Process: Parliament will legislate in 2026 for an Independent Commission on EU Membership Impact (led by the NAO, OBR, and UK Statistics Authority) to audit outcomes of leaving the EU and to produce a single, impartial facts booklet and dataset by mid-2028. A first national referendum in late 2028 asks whether to authorize the government to negotiate EU accession terms. If authorized, negotiations proceed for up to 18 months, followed by a second binding referendum in 2030 on the negotiated terms. Campaign rules include lower spending caps, real-time donation disclosure, a public digital ad library, and equal broadcast access. If either referendum rejects progression, a statutory 10-year moratorium on rejoin applications applies. Justification: ensures informed consent and procedural fairness; trade-off: prolonged uncertainty and administrative cost.

No-Rejoin Decade with Deepened UK–EU Cooperation Package: The UK will legislate a 10-year moratorium on applying to rejoin the EU and instead seek a UK–EU TCA 2.0 by 2027 focused on lowering costs: (a) full veterinary/SPS alignment with joint governance to eliminate most agri-food checks, (b) mutual recognition of conformity assessment to reduce product testing duplication, (c) an expanded trusted trader and customs data pipeline to cut paperwork, (d) youth mobility and cultural exchange visas (up to age 30, two-year stays, reciprocal caps), (e) re-entry to Erasmus+ and strengthened Horizon association, (f) mutual recognition of professional qualifications in key sectors, and (g) bilateral NHS recruitment compacts with fast-track licensing and ethical safeguards. The UK accepts limited dispute resolution tied to the aligned chapters. Trade-offs: partial rule-taking and program fees without a vote in EU institutions, but with immediate reductions in trade frictions and staffing relief.

Brexit Consolidation and Trade Facilitation Plan: Parliament will legislate a 10-year moratorium on applying to rejoin the EU and redirect resources to improving the current settlement. The plan funds a multi-year border modernisation (single customs window, expanded trusted-trader/pre-clearance schemes at EU-facing ports), seeks a comprehensive UK–EU sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) agreement under the TCA to reduce agrifood checks, and introduces a time-limited import cost offset for staple foods while new systems bed in. Trade-off: continued exclusion from the single market and associated rule-making; fiscal cost and only partial relief from trade friction.

Rejoin Roadmap with Confirmatory Referendum: The government will open Article 49 accession talks on a mandate that accepts budget contributions (with a phased ramp-up over five years), ECJ jurisdiction in covered areas, full freedom of movement, and alignment with the acquis, while preserving the Common Travel Area with Ireland and negotiating a phased timetable for Schengen implementation. A draft accession treaty will be put to a legally binding referendum after a six-month independent information process (statutory neutral campaign, audited impact assessments, citizens’ assemblies, and equalised campaign spending rules). Trade-off: reduced unilateral control over regulation and migration and ongoing fiscal contributions, in exchange for restored single market and customs union membership and lower trade barriers.

EEA/EFTA Bridge with Safeguards and Sectoral Protocols: The UK will apply to join EFTA and, via the EEA Agreement, re-enter the single market without joining the EU. The UK will adopt relevant single market rules, contribute to EEA funds, and accept free movement with the option to trigger an Article 112 safeguard in exceptional circumstances. Complementary sectoral accords will be pursued with the EU—including a veterinary/SPS equivalence arrangement and mutual recognition for selected conformity assessment areas—and a mobility partnership targeted at shortage occupations. Trade-off: rule-taking in single market areas and continued customs formalities (the EEA is not a customs union), but quicker reduction in paperwork and barriers for services and many goods.

The UK will submit an Article 49 application to rejoin the EU by Q1 2027, seeking full membership by 2032. The government will accept restoration of free movement, standard budget contributions, and a roadmap to Schengen participation, and will commit to meeting euro convergence criteria without an adoption timetable. A 'Fair Single Market Act' will be passed to pair reaccession with stronger domestic worker rights (sectoral collective bargaining coverage targets, minimum standards on platform work), a £10bn annual green industrial strategy aligned with EU state-aid rules, and automatic recognition of EU professional qualifications. The plan prioritizes rapid easing of labour shortages, re-entry into Erasmus+/Horizon Europe, and integration into EU climate instruments; the tradeoff is reduced unilateral regulatory discretion and net contributions.

Parliament will legislate a two-stage, binding referendum on EU membership in 2028: Stage 1 (June 2027–February 2028) establishes an Independent Referendum Commission to publish a court-verifiable fact audit of Brexit impacts, mandate equal broadcast time and spending caps, and convene a UK-wide citizens' assembly to draft an impartial voter guide. Stage 2 (May 2028) asks two questions on the same ballot: (A) Authorize the government to pursue EU reaccession negotiations; (B) Pre-approve acceptance of free movement and budget contributions as negotiation baselines. Passage requires a simple UK-wide majority plus a majority in at least three of the four nations. If A and B pass, the government must apply within 90 days; if A fails, a five-year moratorium on membership applications is enacted.

The government will rule out applying to rejoin the EU for the next full Parliament and instead implement a 2026–2030 UK–EU Resilience Package: negotiate a comprehensive SPS/veterinary agreement to cut border checks on food and medical inputs by 80%; sign MRAs for medicines, medical devices, and pharmaceuticals batch testing; establish a reciprocal 24-month Youth and Essential Skills Mobility scheme capped at 50,000 visas per side for health, social care, and STEM; link the UK ETS to the EU ETS and align with the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism; associate to the EU Civil Protection Mechanism and deepen Horizon Europe participation; invest £3bn over four years in domestic training for care and construction. This reduces frictions and shortages without surrendering formal membership, but requires meaningful regulatory alignment in covered sectors.

The UK will enact a Rejoin Moratorium and Rural Renewal Act: a 10-year statutory bar on applying to rejoin the EU (2026–2036), alongside a £2.5bn, five-year agricultural sovereignty program to restore 200,000 km of hedgerows and 10,000 ha of traditional orchards, replace retained EU farm rules with UK-designed schemes, and a £1bn Export Friction Fund to help SMEs meet EU border requirements; tradeoff: continued non-tariff barriers with the EU and foregone single-market access for services.

The UK will hold a two-stage, evidence-led referendum on EU re-accession: (1) by Q4 2027, an independent European Impact Commission will publish audited assessments of effects on the UK, the EU, and key trading partners, run regional citizens’ assemblies, and release accessible datasets and household-level impact tools; (2) in Q1 2028, a Stage-1 vote to authorize an application (simple majority UK-wide); (3) if negotiations succeed, a Stage-2 ratification vote by 2030 requiring a UK-wide majority and separate majorities in England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland; tradeoff: longer timeline and political uncertainty during negotiations.

The UK will apply to rejoin the EU with a conditional mandate: retain sterling with a formal commitment not to adopt the euro for at least 15 years (review in 2041); Schengen opt-out with continued participation in Europol/Prüm; re-enter the customs union and single market with full regulatory alignment and ECJ jurisdiction limited to single-market areas; negotiate a UK Agri-Environment Protocol within the CAP to allow nationally tailored eco-schemes for hedgerows and traditional orchards; accept free movement and mutual recognition of qualifications; create a £3bn SME Adjustment Fund and £500m border infrastructure upgrade; target accession by 2031; tradeoffs: higher annual budget contributions, migration and regulatory alignment obligations, and limited scope to set unilateral budget caps.

The government will introduce an EU Rejoin Roadmap in 2026: a cross-party commission and citizens’ assemblies will produce a White Paper by Q2 2027; ministers will seek an indicative pre-accession framework from the EU covering budget contributions, acceptance of the acquis, and transitional arrangements (including a 24-month phased restoration of freedom of movement and timelines for re-entering the customs union and single market). A binding national referendum will be held in June 2028 on those specific terms, with a double-lock requiring both a UK-wide majority and separate majorities in each of the four nations. If approved, the UK will apply under Article 49 in 2028 with a target re-accession date of 2031, committing to ECJ jurisdiction and eventual euro adoption when convergence criteria are met. Tradeoffs include higher budget payments and loss of unilateral regulatory and migration control in exchange for frictionless trade, labour mobility, and closer regional security cooperation.

The UK will negotiate a UK–EU Mobility and Trade Stabilisation Package in 2026 that does not require rejoining: dynamic alignment on sanitary and phytosanitary rules to cut border checks and food costs; a reciprocal Youth Mobility scheme (18–30, two years) and a targeted Essential Skills visa (three years, renewable) for shortage occupations; mutual recognition of professional qualifications in health, construction, and digital; re-association to Erasmus+ and long-term association to Horizon Europe; and green-lane upgrades at key roll-on/roll-off ports and the short straits. An SME support fund will help firms adapt to new paperwork. Tradeoffs include reduced scope for future regulatory divergence and higher short-term administrative costs to implement alignment and mobility systems.

Parliament will enact a Sovereignty and Global Trade Consolidation Act in 2026 that rules out applying to rejoin the EU for 15 years and requires any future application to be preceded by a 60% supermajority referendum. The Act prioritizes non-EU trade expansion: full CPTPP implementation; a fast-track program for India, Gulf, and US agreements; a £5bn customs digitization and port modernization fund; and a five-year Skills and Automation package for agriculture, logistics, and social care to reduce reliance on EU labour, alongside seasonal worker schemes sourced globally. The UK will pursue new mutual recognition agreements and UKCA-led standards to speed global market access. Tradeoffs include persistent frictions with EU trade partners and transitional costs for firms adjusting supply chains.

The UK will enact a 10-year Sovereignty and Rural Restoration Act that rules out applying to rejoin the EU before 2036 (unless overturned by a two-thirds Commons vote and a national referendum), and redirects former EU contribution equivalents into a Rural Fund to replant 200,000 km of hedgerows and 10,000 hectares of traditional orchards, revise farm payments to reward British landscape features, and create a domestic hospitality workforce plan (training grants, apprenticeships, and a seasonal worker scheme sourced outside the EU). Tradeoff: higher short-term costs and continued non-tariff frictions with the EU, with slower relief for Northern Ireland than full EU alignment.

The Government will launch an EU Rejoin Roadmap: a 12-month citizens’ assembly and independent fact-checking office culminating in a 2026 referendum on opening accession talks; if approved, negotiate re-accession on terms that include full single market participation, acceptance of the acquis, freedom of movement, ECJ jurisdiction over EU law, and budget contributions, alongside a Domestic Transition Fund for housing, skills, and border systems, and explicit protocols to remove checks in the Irish Sea by returning to the customs union. A confirmatory referendum will be held on the final treaty before ratification.

The UK will not seek to rejoin the EU but will negotiate a UK–EU Economic Partnership 2.0 comprising a permanent customs union, dynamic alignment with EU sanitary and phytosanitary rules, and a targeted Labour Mobility Compact (3–5 year visas tied to shortage occupations in hospitality, tourism, and care, with mutual recognition of qualifications), to eliminate most GB–NI checks and reduce business frictions while retaining domestic control over broader migration and non–single-market policies. Tradeoff: alignment without a vote on EU rules and ongoing financial contributions to joint programs.
